RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Kartli in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Mtskheta Royal Seat, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Kartli was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Mtskheta Royal Seat, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Mule drivers lead their strings up the gorge road toward Mtskheta, the wine casks rocking in their frames. Each guard walks beside the load with a spear across his shoulder, watching the ravine for bandits. His pay is a few coins and a share of the toll, and he counts the days until the caravan reaches the royal town.

Inside the stone storehouse at Mtskheta, the steward measures wine, salt, and iron against the tolls owed to the crown. Each caravan crossing the mountain passes pays a duty in kind, and the best casks are set aside for the court. He keeps careful notes of every merchant who delays payment, because the royal officials will ask for them.
